title: Higher incidence of bone stress injuries with increasing female athlete triad-related risk factors: a prospective multisite study of exercising girls and women
authors: Barrack MT, Gibbs JC, De Souza MJ, Williams NI, Nichols JF, Rauh MJ, Nattiv A
population: 259 physically active girls and women (mean age 18.1 y) in 4 cohorts, competitive and recreational
findings: 28 participants (10.8%) incurred a bone stress injury (BSI) during prospective follow-up.
Single factors significantly associated with BSI: at least 12 h/week of purposeful exercise (14.7%), BMI below 21.0 kg/m2 (15.3%) and low bone mass (BMD Z-score below -1.0; 21.0%).

Strongest combinations: low BMD + at least 12 h/week exercise gave 29.7% incidence (OR 5.1, 95% CI 2.2-12.1); at least 12 h/week + leanness sport/activity + dietary restraint gave 46.2% (OR 8.7, 95% CI 2.7-28.3).
Risk rose from about 15-20% for single factors to 30-50% for combined triad-related factors, supporting cumulative risk as factors accumulate.
limitations: Mean age 18, mixed sports, 28 events so combined estimates are imprecise; not ultrarunners or older adults.
implications: Implement a cumulative BSI-risk flag counting factors (weekly training time 12 h or more, BMI below 21, menstrual irregularity or amenorrhoea, dietary restraint, prior BSI or known low BMD). At 2 or more factors, cap weekly volume increases below the default progression; the size of the cap is a design choice.
Apply tighter vigilance at 12 h/week or more, which many 100-mile build phases reach; ask about focal bone pain and prompt medical review before further increases.
Do not generalise the BMI 21 cut-off to older athletes or to males.

verification.notes: Crossref matches (Am J Sports Med, 2014-02, Barrack). All numbers confirmed in Europe PMC abstract (PMID 24567250); added the OR 8.7 CI (2.7-28.3) that the abstract does state.
